chief_complaint: creatinine rise 48 hours after coronary angiogram
hpi_details: A 68-year-old female presents to the clinic with creatinine rise 48 hours after coronary angiogram. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: wonders if the dye used in her heart procedure could be the cause
concerns: She is worried her kidneys have suffered permanent damage and she will end up dependent on dialysis.
expectations: She hopes to receive IV fluids to flush out her system so she can safely return home this afternoon.

available_results.test: Serum creatinine 48 hours after coronary angiography
available_results.note: Baseline creatinine before contrast exposure was 1.0 mg/dL.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Contrast-Induced Nephropathy is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes IV isotonic fluid hydration, avoidance of further nephrotoxic exposures, and close monitoring of urine output and creatinine until renal function recovers, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: creatinine rise 48 hours after coronary angiogram

Key HPI features: A 68-year-old female presents to the clinic with creatinine rise 48 hours after coronary angiogram. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: BP 128/78, HR 76, euvolemic, no edema. Labs: Serum creatinine rose from a baseline of 1.0 mg/dL to 1.6 mg/dL at 48 hours post-procedure (meeting AKI criteria), urine output mildly decreased, urinalysis with rare granular casts and no red cell casts or eosinophils, FENa <1%. Received approximately 150 mL of iodinated contrast during the angiogram.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Contrast-Induced Nephropathy.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Cholesterol embolization syndrome without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Anuria — suggests a more severe process.
management_principles: Provide IV isotonic fluids (e.g., normal saline) for volume expansion and hold nephrotoxic medications (NSAIDs, additional contrast, certain antibiotics)
Monitor daily urine output and serum creatinine until renal function stabilizes or returns to baseline
Refer to nephrology if creatinine continues to rise, oliguria/anuria develops, or renal replacement therapy is being considered
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for Kidney Disease

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: creatinine rise 48 hours after coronary angiogram

A 68-year-old female underwent a coronary angiogram with iodinated contrast 48 hours ago for evaluation of chest pain; routine follow-up labs show a rise in creatinine. Reports mild fatigue but denies decreased urine output, flank pain, or swelling.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: BP 128/78, HR 76, euvolemic, no edema. Labs: Serum creatinine rose from a baseline of 1.0 mg/dL to 1.6 mg/dL at 48 hours post-procedure (meeting AKI criteria), urine output mildly decreased, urinalysis with rare granular casts and no red cell casts or eosinophils, FENa <1%. Received approximately 150 mL of iodinated contrast during the angiogram.
reference_soap.assessment: Contrast-induced nephropathy, based on the temporal rise in creatinine within 48-72 hours of iodinated contrast exposure during coronary angiography, without evidence of an alternative cause (no eosinophilia, no red cell casts, FENa <1%).
reference_soap.plan: 1. Provide IV isotonic fluids for volume expansion and hold nephrotoxic medications. 2. Monitor daily urine output and serum creatinine until renal function stabilizes. 3. Refer to nephrology if creatinine continues to rise, oliguria develops, or renal replacement therapy is being considered.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Contrast-Induced Nephropathy
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Contrast-Induced Nephropathy
Implement evidence-based management plan: IV hydration, monitor urine output and creatinine

teaching.one_liner: Intravascular contrast used during a coronary angiogram directly injures the renal tubules in susceptible patients, causing a rise in creatinine 24-72 hours after the procedure.
red_flags: Anuria — suggests a more severe process

must_ask.say: When did you have the angiogram, and when did your kidney numbers change?
Did you have any kidney problems before this procedure?
What medications were you taking around the time of the procedure?
How much fluid have you been drinking?

history.answer: I came in because the doctor called to say my kidney numbers went up on the blood test I had two days after my heart procedure.
I had a coronary angiogram two days ago, and my blood test this morning showed my kidney level jumped up.
I do not have any pain in my kidneys or back, just a general feeling of mild fatigue that started yesterday.
I just feel somewhat washed out and tired, but otherwise I don't feel sharp pain or sick to my stomach.
The tiredness started yesterday morning and has felt slightly more noticeable today, but my kidney numbers were fine before the procedure.
Resting helps my tiredness a bit, but nothing seems to change my kidney lab values.
My urine looks clear, though I feel like I might be peeing slightly less often than usual today.
No, I have had no fever, chills, or night sweats at all.
No, I have not noticed any swelling in my legs, ankles, or around my eyes.
No, I have had no chest pain, shortness of breath, palpitations, or cough since the procedure.
No, I have had no nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or belly pain.
No, my skin looks completely normal, with no rash, itching, or purple spots on my toes.
I had a coronary angiogram exactly 48 hours ago to check out some chest tightness, and they used an imaging dye during it.
They told me my kidney test was completely normal before the angiogram, with a creatinine around 1.0.
I drank some water before and after the angiogram, but I was fasting for several hours right before it began.
No, I did not take any painkillers like ibuprofen or any other medicines around the time of the procedure.
No, I have never had kidney problems, abnormal kidney numbers, or high blood pressure in the past.
I have just been resting and drinking extra water today after the clinic nurse called me about the test results.
I have been taking it easy at home today because of the mild fatigue, but I can still do my daily chores.
I wonder if the contrast dye they injected into my blood vessels during the heart test could have irritated my kidneys.
I'm frightened that this sudden jump in my kidney numbers means permanent damage and that I'll end up hooked up to a dialysis machine.
I'm hoping an IV fluid bag will flush out my system so my numbers look better and I can go home today.
I have generally been very healthy with no chronic medical conditions or high blood pressure.
I have never had any surgeries or hospital admissions other than the angiogram two days ago.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter painkillers, or herbal supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medications or foods.
I have never smoked cigarettes in my life.
I only drink a glass of wine on social occasions once or twice a month, and nothing since the procedure.
I am a retired teacher living with my husband in a house, and I live an independent life.
There is no family history of kidney disease, kidney failure, or dialysis.

exam.finding: Alert, comfortable, and in no acute distress; appears well-hydrated.
Blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, heart rate 76 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, temperature 36.8°C, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Conjunctivae are pink and sclerae are anicteric without pallor or jaundice.
Jugular venous pressure is normal at approximately 2 cm above the sternal angle; no jugular venous distension.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs heard.
Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally with vesicular breath sounds; no crackles or wheezes.
Abdomen is soft, non-tender, and flat; no guarding or palpable masses.
No costovertebral angle tenderness on gentle percussion bilaterally.
Femoral, popliteal, dorsalis pedis, and posterior tibial pulses are 2+ and symmetric bilaterally; no femoral bruits.
No pretibial or ankle edema bilaterally; calves are soft and non-tender.
Skin is warm and dry without rash, petechiae, livedo reticularis, or blue toe discoloration.
